newsitem.title: IRAN: Iran's Khatami calls for "fresh" foreign policy.
newsitem.headline: Iran's Khatami calls for "fresh" foreign policy.

text.p: President Mohammad Khatami of Iran told a parliament session debating his cabinet nominees on Tuesday that the Islamic republic needed a "fresh presence" in its foreign relations.
"In foreign relations we need an active and fresh presence based on our independence and national interests," the moderate Shi'ite Moslem cleric said.
"It is important for us to defuse tensions and seek friendship and brotherhood in the international arena."
Iran's relations with the West are chilly.
"We have to exploit all possibilities to promote and progress our country in the world based upon the three principles of dignity, wisdom and expediency," he said.
Khatami was addressing the Majlis, or parliament, just after it opened debate on his proposed cabinet. It is expected to vote on the 22 nominees on Wednesday.
Khatami, 54, was likely to see at least one of his nominees rejected by the Islamic conservatives who dominate the Majlis in the capital Tehran.
The final make-up of the cabinet is seen as crucial in setting the reform tone of Khatami's four-year term.
"The Majlis (parliament) will approve most of the nominees, but a few who are not qualified will be rejected," rightist deputy Samad Qasempour told the Iran News on Tuesday.

Khatami told the 270-seat parliament: "The two major principles of all (my) plans and programmes are seeking the rule of law and attracting people's participation in political, social and cultural fields.

"As the elected president of the people I am here in the house of the people (parliament) to present the names and the programmes of my colleagues whose success in serving the people depends on the representatives of the people," Khatami said.

"We have had many crises in the past years. Now it's the era of consolidating and stabilising the Islamic republic," he said. "This requires a powerful state but the basis of a powerful state is proper relations with the people so that the system should be based on law."
Khatami was sworn into office on August 4 after being swept to power in national elections last May with the votes of Iranian youth, women and middle classes.
They saw in him a leader able to inject social and economic freedoms into the stern 18-year-old Islamic Republic, whose population is 60 million.

Despite the expected loss of at least one minister in a sensitive domestic portfolio, Khatami will still emerge with the majority of his cabinet largely intact and his election mandate for change undamaged, analysts said.
But ultimate power, especially in foreign relations, in Iran rests firmly in the hands of the supreme Islamic leader, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei.
Khatami has said he will respect the decision of the parliament and has a list of alternatives for cabinet posts.
Strong opposition was expected from conservative factions in parliament to Khatami's proposed minister of culture, Ayatollah Mohajerani, and interior minister, Abdollah Nouri.

The Culture Ministry has emerged as a battleground between Khatami backers who want to breathe more freedoms into Iranian society and conservatives who see the ministry as the main weapon against a "Western cultural invasion."
The ministry has power over the degree of diversity in media, books, films and music permitted in Iran.
Mohajerani in particular has become a lightning rod for conservatives and radical hardliners for his support in 1990 of a resumption of talks with the United States.
The Interior Ministry has influence over the conduct of parliamentary elections and the naming of provincial governors.
